parsed.explanation: The combined regime pairs a protective-leaning division with a hostile national layer the traveller cannot avoid. At entry and in any federal checkpoint, custody, or fraud-referral interaction, the national regime imposes universal exposures: passports must show sex assigned at birth, X markers are blocked, officers are instructed to refuse cases where 'reasonable doubt' about sex exists, and detention placement and national corrections policy are documented as harmful with sexual abuse reported. Some orders are enjoined and litigation is live, so recourse is partial and contested, not established as working for travellers. The division itself adds real mitigation: no bathroom or facility ban, no drag restriction, marker changes possible in limited cases, adult care accessible, marriage recognised, an executive nondiscrimination order, patchwork municipal protections, and a jail placement in the documented arrest case that still meant a trans woman held in a men's ward. Exposure is not organised targeting or imprisonment-on-sight; it is recurring unremedied institutional friction plus custody harm risk.

entry_documents.exposure: National passport regime requires birth-sex marker; X markers blocked; visa cable directs refusal on 'reasonable doubt' and possible lifetime fraud finding; reported confiscations stranding travellers; scanner/pat-down outing risk documented.
entry_documents.protection: X passports issued before Feb 2025 remain valid until expiry; passport policy under active court challenge; legal-aid FAQ exists.
entry_documents.interaction: Document mismatch at entry can feed a federal fraud investigation or refusal; division rules cannot displace national screening.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: National corrections policy mandates hair-cutting, hormone withdrawal and psychiatric substitution; immigration custody reports of forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and sexual abuse of trans men; Bureau stopped reporting trans prisoner counts.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: Not documented at national level; division prison statute guarantees hormone therapy per 2011–2012 rulings.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: Any federal detention (immigration, federal offence) places the traveller under the hostile national custody regime regardless of division law.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: Facility bans in ~22 state/provinces nationwide, criminal exposure in 4; documented trespass arrest of a trans woman, held 24h in a men's ward.
federal_state_facilities.protection: This division has no facility ban, no restrictive sex definition, no drag restriction; state employment/services nondiscrimination order.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Traveller is exposed only when crossing into banning state/provinces or federal facilities; within the division, facilities follow identity.

care_services.exposure: National pressure shut two hospital systems' youth pharmacologic care; national orders frame minor care as 'mutilation'; national rules would bar public insurance reimbursement for under-18s.
care_services.protection: Division bans nothing: adult care uninterrupted; governor vetoed youth-care and sports bans; insurance exclusions barred; coalition challenging national declaration.
care_services.interaction: Adult traveller's care is secure in the division; a travelling minor's pharmacologic care is disrupted by national funding leverage despite no state ban.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National orders use 'gender ideology' and 'radically pro-transgender' framings; schools/teachers face prosecution for facilitating social transition; subpoenaed hospital records of under-19 patients.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: Several orders blocked or enjoined; counterterrorism document states powers not used against mere disagreement; division governor publicly welcoming.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: A travelling minor's use of preferred name/pronouns could implicate national school-prosecution directives; litigation unresolved.

minors_guardians.exposure: Youth care paused at two hospital systems; teachers facilitating transition face prosecution risk under national order; national record subpoenas; proposed insurance bar.
minors_guardians.protection: No state ban; vetoes; care-access groups; school sports bans vetoed; unresolved challenges.
minors_guardians.interaction: Guardian's minor may access mental health services but not paused pharmacologic care; schools remain under national investigative threat.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: GI not covered by state hate-crime statute; no statewide GI nondiscrimination law; one documented restroom arrest with handcuffing and men's-ward holding.
street_violence_police_response.protection: SO hate-crime coverage used as charging route; municipal GI ordinances cover 21% of population; city stopped recording victim gender to avoid misgendering; national hate-crime statute covers GI.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Local police response varies by city; state-level recourse thinner than in fully protective states.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Passport policy unresolved; national health rules pending; hospital pause status unknown; marker-change documentation standard unstated; no state shield law.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Active litigation, multistate coalition, legal-aid FAQ, functioning state courts (hormone-therapy rulings enforced).
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Practical exposure depends on which measures are operative at travel time; several national rules may be enjoined at any given moment.

anchor_checks.comparison: 0.35-A imposes a universal, court-confirmed birth-sex facility exclusion with no relief anywhere. Here the division has no facility ban and documented vetoes protect care; the universal exposures sit at the national border/documents/custody layer with contested rather than confirmed litigation. Materially better than 0.35-A.

Like 0.55-D, exposures are institutional and recurring but partially corrected or contested, service life is mostly ordinary, and enforcement is uneven. The national document regime is a heavier, more universal exposure than 0.55-D's hotel-refusal pattern, but the division's protections are stronger. Roughly comparable, slightly heavier exposure.

0.75-C has a dead-letter statute, accepted documents, and functioning remedies with only open questions. Here the document regime is an active, enforced national restriction reaching every traveller, plus documented custody abuse — a known exposure, not an open question — so this jurisdiction sits clearly below 0.75-C.

0.65-A pairs accepted borders with working, if uneven, remedies. The national layer here (marker bans, fraud-referral cable, custody harm) is worse than 0.65-A's border acceptance, but the division's veto record, facility access and care access exceed 0.65-A's baseline; the mix lands between 0.55 and 0.65.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller's journey splits into two regimes. Within the division, documented practice is protective-leaning: no facility ban, identity-congruent access, adult care continuity, recognised marriage, municipal nondiscrimination, and courts that have enforced hormone access in custody. Across the national layer — entry screening, passports, any federal detention, and care for a travelling minor — the operative rules are actively hostile: birth-sex markers enforced, X markers blocked, 'reasonable doubt' refusal instructions, documented custody abuse and halted reporting, and funding-leverage disruption of youth care. These national exposures are universal for every trans visitor at the border and are only partially mitigated by ongoing, unresolved litigation. The combination — a welcoming division under an enforced hostile parent regime with contested remedies — places the jurisdiction in elevated risk, above the fully protective 0.65–0.75 tier and clearly above unremedied-exposure 0.35 profiles, at approximately 0.58.
